# Nethra and the Ironcloak — Narrative Script

*Audio: 03_Nethra_and_the_Ironcloak.mp3 — July 22, 2026*

---

Kirivis, the Demon King, was the greatest ruler the Demon Continent had ever known. A warrior-scholar of the Bjor subrace, he built roads across the wasteland, improved medicine, stopped famines, and united warring tribes. He never married. But he adopted two children: a demon boy named Maoth and a human girl he found abandoned near the Lyrical Forest. Her name was Nethra.

What Kirivis did not know was that Nethra's soul was a fragment of Xiumi — the twelve-year-old girl who had saved the Glorious Alliance eight thousand years earlier. The soul fragment had drifted across the ages, seeking a vessel, and found one in the infant Kirivis discovered.

Kirivis also possessed a secret: the Glowing Tablet, a Hybrian artifact that fed him fragments of truth for sixty years. It made him paranoid. It also made him correct. He spent a decade studying it, pretending to be insane so no one would take his ravings seriously. What he discovered shattered him.

The Shadows were real. They had infiltrated Baoth. They were trying to possess the dragon king Goldenborn. They had been playing this game for six thousand years.

Kirivis attacked Baoth without warning. No explanation, no declaration. A forty-five year war that consumed the continent. At its end, he was beheaded by Rulfred, a Shadow agent known as the Beast. He died a villain in the eyes of the world — and a hero to those who knew the truth.

Nethra marched to avenge him. The spirits of the Lyrical Forest — the souls of fallen coalition soldiers from the Last Great War — gave her a device. A gift from three million years of war. She detonated it in Baoth. The city was destroyed. The Goldenborn dragon fell.

And Nethra was transformed. She became a different type of Shadow — one that could walk among them undetected. She secretly founded the Ironcloak, the order dedicated to bringing humanity to the truth. To this day, she walks among the Shadows, unknown, waiting.
